hero.headline: U.S. Strikes Iran Military Targets for Second Time This Week
hero.body:
The United States conducted new strikes on military sites in southern Iran on Wednesday, marking the second such attack in three days. According to U.S. officials, the strikes targeted attack drones and a drone ground control station that Iran had launched.

The military operations were described as defensive in nature. Officials stated the attacks focused on four one-way attack drones, hitting military installations in Iran's southern region.

The strikes come while diplomatic negotiations between Washington and Tehran continue, though a cease-fire between the countries remains fragile. The two nations have been engaged in talks aimed at resolving a three-month conflict that has involved multiple regional actors. The latest military operations threaten to complicate these ongoing diplomatic efforts, even as negotiations have stretched over an extended period without producing a final agreement.

Iran's foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, said his government expects to have a draft counterproposal ready within days following nuclear talks with the U.S. this week. During indirect discussions in Geneva with Trump's special envoy Steve Witkoff and son-in-law Jared Kushner, Araghchi stated the sides had reached an understanding on main "guiding principles." He indicated more talks could occur in about a week.

President Trump has signaled he is considering limited military strikes to pressure Iran into making concessions on its nuclear program. He ordered a massive buildup of naval forces in the Middle East, including repositioning aircraft carriers and other warships. Trump gave Iran a deadline of 10 to 15 days to make a deal or face "really bad things."

Araghchi countered that there is no "military solution" to Iran's nuclear program. "That has been tested last year," he said, referring to strikes on Iranian facilities. "They couldn't kill our nuclear programme."

During Geneva discussions, the U.S. did not seek zero uranium enrichment and Iran did not offer to suspend enrichment. Araghchi explained the focus shifted to ensuring Iran's nuclear program remains peaceful. A White House official responded that "the president has been clear that Iran cannot have nuclear weapons or the capacity to build them, and that they cannot enrich uranium."

Oil markets responded to the strikes with price increases, as traders expressed renewed concerns about potential disruptions to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. The waterway is critical for global energy supplies.

The conflict has affected neighboring countries. Kuwait reported being targeted by missiles and drones, though no attribution was provided. Israel has intensified military operations in southern Lebanon during the same period, with Lebanese residents expressing doubt that any U.S.-Iran agreement would bring peace to their country.

cards.headline: U.S. strikes Iranian drone site as Trump maintains demands
cards.body:
The United States conducted airstrikes on an Iranian military facility after downing Iranian attack drones, according to U.S. officials. The strikes represent continued military action as President Trump holds firm on what officials describe as maximum demands in negotiations with Tehran.

The timing of the military operations comes as Trump expressed indifference to pressure from some members of his party about conducting strikes before midterm elections. The president has maintained his hardline position on Iran policy despite criticism about potential political consequences.

Trump signaled that he will not lift a naval blockade on Iranian ports until securing a deal addressing Iran's nuclear program. In an interview with Axios, the president said the blockade was more effective than bombing, stating "They are choking like a stuffed pig. And it is going to be worse for them."

This position has had significant economic consequences. Brent crude oil jumped to its highest level in nearly four years, hitting $119.76 a barrel. The price increase reflects market concerns about disruptions to the Strait of Hormuz, a critical shipping channel for global energy supplies. Oil prices rose approximately 7 percent following Trump's comments about extending the blockade.

The blockade's economic impact extends beyond energy markets. The United States has become a net exporter of crude oil for the first time since World War Two, shipping record volumes to international refiners scrambling for supplies. This has led to significant drops in domestic crude oil inventories, according to the Energy Information Administration.

The broader conflict has created economic strain across multiple sectors. Britain's stock market ended at its lowest close since March, with the FTSE 100 dropping 1.16 percent. UK borrowing costs are rising as oil and gas price increases threaten to push up inflation. The yield on two-year UK government bonds hit its highest level since March.

Financial institutions have begun accounting for conflict-related losses. Lloyds Bank took a 151 million pound charge to cover economic damage from the Iran war. Middle East conflicts have also knocked UK exports to the region down by a fifth.

In a contrasting development, pharmaceutical company AstraZeneca announced a surprise 300 million pound investment in the UK. The company said it would unfreeze a paused 200 million pound expansion in Cambridge and invest 100 million pounds into its Macclesfield site. This investment represents a turnaround after the company paused large-scale projects previously.

The decision signals potential recovery in UK life sciences investment. Since a UK-U.S. drug pricing deal reached in December, companies have invested 1.4 billion pounds in UK life sciences. The pharmaceutical industry's trade association described the recent months as "remarkable" for UK life sciences investment.

Talks between Washington and Tehran have continued for three months without breakthrough. Military operations continue alongside diplomatic channels as both sides navigate the conflict.

cards.headline: Justice Department opens criminal investigation into Trump accuser E. Jean Carroll
cards.body:
The Department of Justice has launched a criminal investigation into E. Jean Carroll, who accused President Trump of sexual assault, according to multiple reports.

CNN first reported Wednesday night that the investigation focuses on whether Carroll committed perjury while speaking at a deposition during her two civil lawsuits against Trump. The probe represents a significant escalation in the legal battle between Carroll and the president.

Carroll won two civil cases against Trump. In the first case, a jury found Trump liable for sexual abuse and defamation. In the second case, a jury awarded Carroll additional damages for defamation after Trump continued to deny her allegations.

The criminal investigation comes as Trump has repeatedly denied Carroll's accusations and criticized the civil verdicts against him. The Justice Department has not publicly commented on the scope or timeline of the investigation.

Perjury charges require prosecutors to prove that a witness knowingly made false statements under oath during official proceedings. The penalty for perjury in federal court can include fines and imprisonment.

Carroll originally came forward in 2019 with allegations that Trump sexually assaulted her in a department store dressing room in the mid-1990s. Trump denied the allegations and said he had never met Carroll, despite a photograph showing them together.

The civil trials included testimony from both Carroll and Trump, as well as other witnesses. Carroll testified under oath during depositions and at trial about her allegations and the impact of Trump's public denials.

The investigation adds another layer to the ongoing legal confrontations between Trump and his accusers. It also raises questions about the Justice Department's independence, as the agency now investigates someone who successfully sued the current president in civil court.

Neither the Justice Department nor Carroll's legal team has made public statements about the investigation. The timing and potential outcomes of the probe remain uncertain.

cards.headline: US military shoots down four Iranian drones, strikes ground station
cards.teaser: American forces intercepted Iranian attack drones targeting a commercial ship and destroyed a drone launch facility.
cards.body:
The U.S. military intercepted four Iranian attack drones and destroyed a ground control station in Bandar Abbas that was preparing to launch a fifth drone. The drones threatened a commercial vessel in the Strait of Hormuz.

This represents the second military engagement between U.S. and Iranian forces within 48 hours, occurring amid ongoing negotiations between the two countries during a fragile ceasefire in the three-month conflict.

cards.headline: Uganda Closes Border With Congo as Ebola Cases Rise
cards.teaser: Uganda shut its border with the Democratic Republic of Congo after Ebola cases were confirmed in the capital Kampala.
cards.body:
Uganda closed its border with the Democratic Republic of Congo amid a worsening Ebola outbreak in the eastern region. Suspected cases in the DRC have exceeded 900, with 119 suspected deaths reported. The World Health Organization has assessed the outbreak as posing a "very high" risk within the country, though it notes the global spread risk remains low.

Uganda has confirmed seven Ebola cases in Kampala, the capital. The country has implemented disease surveillance systems to monitor the situation and prevent further transmission across the border.

cards.headline: Former CIA officer arrested with $40 million in gold bars at home
cards.teaser: Federal authorities arrested a former CIA official after discovering approximately 300 gold bars valued at $40 million in his residence.
cards.body:
The FBI arrested David Rush, a former CIA officer, after prosecutors said he stole $40 million worth of gold bars from the agency. Authorities recovered approximately 300 gold bars from his home.

Rush had worked as a government official before his arrest. Federal prosecutors accused him of taking the gold bars from the CIA during his time with the agency. The arrest represents one of the largest alleged thefts of physical assets from a U.S. intelligence organization.

cards.headline: Washington paper mill disaster leaves 11 presumed dead
cards.teaser: A chemical tank rupture at a Longview paper mill may be the deadliest industrial accident in modern Washington state history, according to the governor.
cards.body:
A chemical tank ruptured at a Nippon paper mill in Longview, Washington, resulting in one confirmed death and nine people missing. Nine others sustained injuries in the incident.

The rupture released white liquor, a caustic chemical used in paper production. Washington's governor called the disaster a potential "deadliest industrial tragedy in modern Washington state history."

cards.headline: Google engineer charged with insider trading after betting $1.2 million on Polymarket
cards.body:
Federal prosecutors in New York charged a longtime Google employee with insider trading after he allegedly used internal company data to place bets worth $1.2 million on the prediction market platform Polymarket.

The engineer worked in information security at Google. Prosecutors allege he accessed confidential information through his position at the company and used that data to inform bets on Polymarket, a platform where users wager on the outcomes of real-world events.

The charges were filed in New York and represent the latest case of authorities targeting alleged misuse of insider information. The case marks an unusual application of insider trading laws to prediction market betting rather than traditional stock trading.

Polymarket operates as a decentralized prediction market where participants bet on outcomes ranging from political elections to economic indicators. The platform has grown in popularity as an alternative way to gauge public sentiment on major events.

Prosecutors did not disclose what specific events the Google employee bet on or what type of internal Google data he allegedly accessed. The charging documents also did not specify the time period during which the alleged trading occurred.

The engineer's employment status at Google following the charges was not made public. Google has not issued a statement about the case or the employee's status with the company.

Insider trading laws traditionally apply to securities markets, where individuals with access to material nonpublic information about publicly traded companies are prohibited from trading on that knowledge. This case extends those principles to prediction markets, where bets function similarly to trades.

The $1.2 million figure represents the total value of bets placed, though it was not clear from available information whether that amount reflected profits, total wagers, or another metric. The specific charges filed against the engineer were not detailed in the available source material.

The case adds to growing regulatory attention on prediction markets and how existing financial laws apply to these newer platforms. Legal experts have debated whether traditional insider trading frameworks adequately cover betting on prediction markets versus conventional securities trading.

cards.headline: Former judges ask court to review Trump IRS settlement creating $1.776 billion fund
cards.teaser: A bipartisan group of former federal judges asked a court to reopen a case involving President Trump's lawsuit against the IRS.
cards.body:
A bipartisan group of former federal judges asked a federal court Wednesday to investigate President Trump's settlement with the Internal Revenue Service. The judges argue that the administration bypassed proper judicial oversight by negotiating the deal outside of court proceedings.

The settlement established a $1.776 billion fund intended to compensate alleged victims of what the administration calls "lawfare and weaponization." California Governor Gavin Newsom announced plans to impose a 100% tax on any payments received by state residents from the fund, seeking to prevent the money from reaching Trump allies and others he views as undeserving recipients.

cards.headline: Record Spring Heat Wave Breaks Temperature Records Across Europe
cards.teaser: An unusually early heat wave shattered records in multiple European capitals, bringing deaths and prompting emergency responses.
cards.body:
Western Europe is experiencing an exceptionally early heat wave that has shattered spring temperature records across the continent. London has recorded temperatures reaching 95 degrees over consecutive days, triggering government warnings. The extreme conditions have resulted in deaths in several European countries.

Scientists attribute the intense heat to a combination of a heat dome and climate change. The buckled jet stream has created unpredictable and extreme weather patterns that are becoming increasingly frequent. Experts warn that these record-breaking temperatures represent a troubling trend of escalating heat events.

cards.headline: Biden sues Justice Department to block interview recordings
cards.teaser: Former President Joe Biden filed a lawsuit against the Justice Department seeking to prevent the release of audio recordings from interviews.
cards.body:
Biden took legal action to stop the Justice Department from releasing audio files of interviews he gave. The lawsuit represents an unusual step of a former president suing the department he once oversaw.

President Trump criticized Biden over the legal filing, accusing him of trying to hide the interview recordings. The Justice Department has not commented on the substance of the recordings or the timeline for their potential release.

cards.headline: Stock markets close at record highs as oil prices fall on Iran war hopes
cards.teaser: The Dow, S&P 500, and Nasdaq all reached record closing levels while oil prices dropped amid expectations for an end to conflict with Iran.
cards.body:
Major US stock indexes reached all-time highs Monday as investors grew optimistic about a potential peace deal between the US and Iran. The Dow Jones Industrial Average, S&P 500, and Nasdaq all posted record closes.

Oil prices tumbled during the session, with Brent crude futures falling 6% to $97.43 a barrel—the lowest level in two weeks—as hopes for an agreement to end the nearly three-month conflict strengthened. Micron Technology extended its gains amid continued momentum in artificial intelligence stocks.

cards.headline: Court orders customs chief to appear over $166 billion in tariff refunds
cards.teaser: A judge demanded the customs chief address compliance issues related to repaying tariffs that were ruled illegal.
cards.body:
A court ordered the head of US Customs to appear at a hearing to address the Trump administration's efforts to refund $166 billion in tariffs that were imposed illegally. The demand for testimony indicated new judicial concern about compliance with refund requirements.

The refunds stem from tariffs that courts determined violated the law. The hearing requirement represented an escalation in judicial oversight of the refund process, with the judge seeking direct answers from the customs chief about the administration's progress in returning the money.

cards.headline: Australia sues 3M for $2 billion over contaminated firefighting foam
cards.body:
The Australian government filed a lawsuit against US manufacturing giant 3M seeking $2 billion in damages over contamination caused by PFAS chemicals in firefighting foam used at dozens of defense sites across the country.

The case centers on per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances, commonly known as PFAS or "forever chemicals," which were present in foam products supplied by 3M. These chemicals earned their nickname because they do not break down naturally in the environment and can persist for decades.

The contamination affected multiple Australian defense facilities where the foam had been deployed. PFAS chemicals have raised health and environmental concerns globally due to their resistance to degradation and their accumulation in soil, water, and living organisms.

The $2 billion lawsuit represents one of the largest legal actions taken by a national government against 3M over PFAS contamination. The company has faced similar litigation in multiple countries as awareness of the chemicals' environmental persistence has grown.

3M, headquartered in Minnesota, manufactures a wide range of industrial and consumer products. The company previously produced firefighting foams containing PFAS for use by military installations, airports, and fire departments around the world.

Australian defense sites used these foam products for firefighting and training exercises over many years. The legal action alleges that this use resulted in widespread contamination of soil and groundwater at the affected locations.

The lawsuit comes as governments worldwide have increased scrutiny of PFAS chemicals and their manufacturers. Several countries have moved to phase out or restrict the use of these substances in firefighting foam and other products.

3M announced in recent years that it would discontinue manufacturing PFAS-based products, though the timeline for complete phase-out varies by product line and region. The company has also faced cleanup costs and legal settlements related to PFAS contamination at sites in the United States and other countries.

The Australian government's legal action seeks to recover costs associated with investigating and remediating the contamination at defense facilities. The case will proceed through Australian courts, though no trial date has been announced.

cards.headline: Georgia coach suggests SEC could leave NCAA over playoff dispute
cards.body:
Georgia head coach Kirby Smart indicated the Southeastern Conference could separate from the NCAA if the league cannot reach an agreement on College Football Playoff terms. Smart made the comments during SEC spring meetings, where conference expansion has dominated discussions.

The possibility of SEC secession emerged as the league debates its future in college athletics governance. The conference has faced challenges in recent playoff negotiations, including a 4-0 record against them by Big Ten teams in head-to-head College Football Playoff matchups over the past three seasons.

SEC Commissioner Greg Sankey has maintained the conference still stands alone despite the Big Ten winning the past three national titles. The competitive landscape has shifted as conference realignment reshapes college football.

Smart's suggestion that the SEC could operate under its own rules reflects broader tensions in college athletics. The spring meetings have turned into what observers describe as a reality check for the current structure of college sports governance.

The comments come as multiple reports indicate the SEC is evaluating its options for future governance structures. The conference would seek to establish its own competitive framework if it cannot secure favorable terms in playoff negotiations.

College Football Playoff expansion remains a central issue in these discussions. Oklahoma athletic director Roger Denny separately noted that playoff expansion could enable scheduling tougher nonconference games and potentially revive rivalry series like the Sooners' matchup against Oklahoma State.

The potential departure would represent a fundamental restructuring of college athletics. The SEC has not provided a timeline for any decision, but Smart's public statements signal the league is prepared to consider alternatives to NCAA membership if necessary.

cards.headline: Appeals court allows pro-Palestinian activist to remain free pending Supreme Court appeal
cards.teaser: A federal appeals panel ruled that Mahmoud Khalil can stay out of custody while challenging his case.
cards.body:
A three-judge panel of the 3rd Circuit Court of Appeals ruled Tuesday that pro-Palestinian activist Mahmoud Khalil can remain free as he takes his case against the Trump administration to the Supreme Court. The panel includes appointees from three different administrations.

Judges Stephanos Bibas, Arianna Freeman and Thomas Hardiman issued the order. Bibas was appointed by President Trump, Freeman by former President George W. Bush, and Hardiman by former President Joe Biden.

cards.headline: Iran Restores Internet Access After 88-Day Shutdown
cards.teaser: The Iranian government allowed citizens to reconnect with the outside world after nearly three months of censored communications.
cards.body:
Iran ended a near-total internet shutdown that had lasted 88 days, allowing its population to access online services again. The government had blocked television, chat services, and most internet connectivity during the period.

Access remains uneven across the country, with not all Iranians able to connect. Citizens who have regained internet access expressed uncertainty about whether the government would maintain the restored connectivity or impose new restrictions.

cards.headline: Lebanese Expect Prolonged Conflict Despite U.S.-Iran Negotiations
cards.teaser: Residents of Lebanon say diplomatic efforts between Washington and Tehran will not bring peace to their country.
cards.body:
Lebanese citizens expressed skepticism that negotiations between the United States and Iran would end fighting in their country. Clashes between Israel and Hezbollah have intensified in southern Lebanon during the broader regional conflict.

Few in Lebanon believe the diplomatic process will bring peace even if the U.S. and Iran reach an agreement. The fighting in the south has continued despite ongoing talks aimed at ending the wider war.

cards.headline: Google employee charged over $1.2 million in prediction market profits
cards.teaser: The Justice Department charged a Google staffer with using insider information to profit from trades on the prediction market platform Polymarket.
cards.body:
Federal prosecutors charged Google employee Michele Spagnuolo with fraud after he allegedly used insider information to make $1.2 million in profits on Polymarket. According to the unsealed complaint, Spagnuolo had access to Google's confidential data about Search-related trends in 2025, which he used to gain an unfair advantage on the prediction market platform.

This marks the second known federal case involving criminal charges for insider trading on a prediction market site. Polymarket allows users to bet on the outcomes of various future events, from elections to corporate decisions.

cards.headline: Ferrari faces backlash over first electric car
cards.teaser: The Italian automaker's initial electric vehicle sparked criticism in Italy and beyond, with memes mocking the model and investors selling stock.
cards.body:
Ferrari's unveiling of its first fully electric car, the Luce model, has sparked significant backlash. The new model divided opinion on social media, with memes mocking the vehicle. Analysts questioned its market appeal, and investors responded by selling Ferrari stock.

The negative reaction reflects broader concerns about the brand's shift away from high-performance gasoline engines. A former Ferrari chairman warned about "the destruction of a legend," highlighting worries that electrification could damage Ferrari's iconic status in the automotive world.

cards.headline: California court rejects Tesla bid to dismiss racial discrimination lawsuit
cards.teaser: A California court denied Tesla's attempt to throw out a racial discrimination lawsuit brought by state civil rights officials.
cards.body:
A California court denied Tesla's motion to dismiss a racial discrimination lawsuit brought by the state's civil rights agency. The ruling clears the path for the case to advance to trial, with proceedings expected to begin in July.

The civil rights agency views the court's decision as a significant victory in its legal challenge against the electric vehicle manufacturer over allegations of racial discrimination at Tesla facilities.

cards.headline: Hurricanes take 3-1 series lead with shutout win over Canadiens
cards.teaser: Frederik Andersen made 18 saves as Carolina moved within one win of the Stanley Cup Final.
cards.body:
Goaltender Frederik Andersen delivered a dominant performance, making 18 saves to shut out the Canadiens and push the Hurricanes within one win of the Stanley Cup Final. The victory gave Carolina a 3-1 series lead in the Eastern Conference Final.

Andersen's shutout marked his third of the postseason. The Hurricanes can clinch their trip to the Finals with a win in Game 5.

cards.headline: Spielberg Says Hollywood Should Never Use AI as Final Word on Creative Decisions
cards.body:
Steven Spielberg spoke out against artificial intelligence in filmmaking during an appearance on Michelle Obama and Craig Robinson's IMO podcast. The director said he opposes AI taking over the creative process in Hollywood.

Spielberg drew a clear line on where he finds AI acceptable. He said the technology can be useful for finding solutions to medical issues. However, he does not want it controlling creative decisions in film production.

The director stated that AI should never serve as the final word on anything creative. He identified this boundary as his primary concern with the technology's role in entertainment.

Spielberg's comments add his voice to ongoing debates in Hollywood about AI's expanding role in the industry. His position reflects concern among filmmakers about preserving human creativity and decision-making in the production process.

The legendary director's remarks come as AI tools become increasingly sophisticated and more widely available to studios and production companies. Various forms of AI are already being used in script analysis, visual effects, and other aspects of filmmaking.

Spielberg has directed numerous acclaimed films over a career spanning more than five decades. His stance carries significant weight in industry discussions about the future of filmmaking technology and creative control.

cards.headline: Senator Andy Kim responds to Homeland Security secretary over detention facility protest
cards.teaser: The New Jersey senator pushed back after being criticized for attending a demonstration outside a migrant facility.
cards.body:
Democratic Sen. Andy Kim of New Jersey responded Wednesday to criticism from Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, who slammed the senator for attending a protest outside a migrant detention facility in New Jersey. During a cabinet meeting at the White House, Mullin said Kim complained about being hit by pepper ball spray at the protest.

Kim fired back at the secretary's comments, stating that the incident was not about him personally. The exchange highlighted tensions between Democratic lawmakers and the Trump administration over immigration enforcement policies.

cards.headline: Jill Biden Says She Feared Husband Was Having Stroke During 2024 Debate
cards.teaser: The former first lady told CBS News she was frightened by Joe Biden's debate performance against Donald Trump.
cards.body:
Jill Biden told CBS News that she was frightened while watching Joe Biden's performance during his 2024 presidential debate against Donald Trump. The former first lady said she had never seen her husband perform that way before or since.

In the interview set to air on Sunday, Biden expressed concern about what she witnessed, describing her reaction as one of fear during the debate.

cards.headline: FIFA investigated over World Cup ticket prices and sales practices
cards.teaser: New York and New Jersey authorities are examining the soccer association after reports that fans were misled about ticket sales and seating.
cards.body:
The attorneys general of New York and New Jersey have launched a joint investigation into FIFA's ticketing practices for the 2026 World Cup. The probe focuses on matches scheduled for MetLife Stadium in East Rutherford, New Jersey, and was announced by New York's Letitia James and New Jersey's Jennifer Davenport.

Fans have reported being misled about seat locations, and authorities are examining whether FIFA's public messaging contributed to inflated ticket prices. The investigation involves a subpoena seeking information about FIFA's ticketing practices and how the organization marketed and sold World Cup tickets to buyers.

cards.headline: Rivian sets June 9 delivery date for first R2 electric SUVs
cards.teaser: The electric vehicle maker will begin customer deliveries of its new R2 SUV on June 9.
cards.body:
Rivian has set June 9 as the delivery date for the first R2 electric SUVs to customers. The company has been working toward this milestone for its newest model.

CEO RJ Scaringe has called the R2 "maybe the most important thing we've launched to date," underscoring its significance to the company's expansion plans.

cards.headline: Phillies pitcher sets franchise record with 44 consecutive scoreless innings
cards.teaser: Cristopher Sanchez broke a record held by Hall of Famer Grover Cleveland Alexander since 1911.
cards.body:
Cristopher Sánchez set a new Phillies franchise record on Wednesday, extending his scoreless innings streak to 44⅔ innings. He surpassed the previous mark held by Hall of Famer Grover Cleveland Alexander, who set the original record in 1911.

Sánchez's achievement represents the longest scoreless streak in Phillies history across the franchise's 115-year existence.

cards.headline: Projected first-round pick Koa Peat stays in NBA draft
cards.teaser: The Arizona forward will forgo his remaining college eligibility.
cards.body:
Arizona forward Koa Peat has declared for the NBA draft, according to ESPN sources. The decision on Wednesday means he is forgoing his remaining college eligibility to pursue a professional basketball career.

Peat is expected to be selected in the first round of the upcoming draft.

cards.headline: Former Super Bowl MVP Von Miller seeks return to Broncos
cards.teaser: The linebacker said he has lobbied Denver coach Sean Payton about rejoining his former team.
cards.body:
Von Miller declared Wednesday that he will definitely play in the 2026 season and has already reached out to Denver Broncos coach Sean Payton about a potential reunion. The Super Bowl MVP is actively pursuing a return to his former team.

Miller's direct approach to the Broncos coaching staff shows his clear interest in rejoining the franchise where he previously won his championship.

cards.headline: Top transfer portal player Milan Momcilovic withdraws from NBA draft
cards.teaser: The former Iowa State forward will return to college basketball next season.
cards.body:
Milan Momcilovic is withdrawing from the NBA draft to continue his college basketball career. The forward, who previously played for Iowa State, was ranked as the top player available in the transfer portal.

After declaring for the NBA draft, Momcilovic decided to return to college rather than pursue a professional career. His agents confirmed the decision to ESPN.

cards.headline: ABC News and National Geographic Lead News Emmy Awards
cards.teaser: ABC World News Tonight won outstanding live news program for the second consecutive year at the 47th annual News Emmys.
cards.body:
ABC News dominated the 47th annual News Emmy Awards with eight wins, capturing the top prize for outstanding live news program. ABC World News Tonight with David Muir secured the award for the second consecutive year.

National Geographic achieved strong recognition at the ceremony with seven News Emmy Awards. The outlet's wins were highlighted by honors for Trafficked with Mariana van Zeller, underscoring the Disney-owned network's competitive performance in television news.

cards.headline: Student Journalist Criticizes CBS News While Accepting Mike Wallace Scholarship
cards.teaser: Santiago Campos called out CBS News during his acceptance speech at the News Emmys, saying the outlet's recent direction damages Mike Wallace's legacy.
cards.body:
Santiago Campos, a senior at District of Columbia International School in Washington, addressed CBS News critically while accepting the Mike Wallace Memorial Scholarship at the News Emmy Awards. The scholarship is named after the veteran CBS journalist.

Former CBS Evening News anchor Scott Pelley presented the award. Campos told the crowd that the recent direction of CBS News stains the legacy of Mike Wallace. The student's remarks drew attention from the News Emmy audience.

cards.headline: Senate Republicans move to support Paxton after divisive Texas primary
cards.teaser: Republican leadership is working to unite the party behind Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton following his primary victory.
cards.body:
Senate Republican leaders are working to rebuild their relationship with Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton following a contentious primary battle. Senate Majority Leader John Thune of South Dakota spoke with Paxton by phone and subsequently endorsed him on a radio show, while also criticizing the Democratic nominee for state attorney general.

The primary contest between Paxton and Sen. John Cornyn was expensive and divisive, costing $130 million. Party leadership now considers Texas essential to their efforts to maintain control of the Senate, prompting senior Republicans to signal their support to major donors.

cards.headline: NASA spacecraft captures detailed Mars images during flyby
cards.teaser: A NASA probe photographed Mars in high resolution while passing the planet on its journey to study a distant asteroid.
cards.body:
NASA's Psyche spacecraft captured detailed images of Mars during a flyby on its way to explore a metal-rich asteroid in the outer solar system. The photographs showcase the Martian south pole and other surface features from a unique vantage point.

The high-resolution images provide scientists with valuable data to study as Psyche continues its multi-year journey toward its primary mission target, the asteroid it was designed to investigate.

cards.headline: Nintendo adds Donkey Kong 64 to Switch Online next week
cards.teaser: The classic Nintendo 64 game Donkey Kong 64 will join the Switch Online library next week.
cards.body:
Nintendo announced it will add Donkey Kong 64 to its Nintendo Switch Online service next week, expanding the platform's collection of classic Nintendo 64 titles. The 1999 adventure game will become available to subscribers who pay for the service tier that includes retro games.

Donkey Kong 64 originally released for the Nintendo 64 console and featured the barrel-throwing ape in a three-dimensional platforming adventure. The addition continues Nintendo's gradual expansion of vintage games available through its online subscription service.

cards.headline: Morris Day Denies Planned Appearance at National Mall Freedom 250 Concert
cards.teaser: The singer said he will not perform at a patriotic festival in Washington despite being listed as a headliner by event organizers.
cards.body:
Morris Day has denied rumors that he and the Time will perform at the Freedom 250 concert scheduled for June 27 on the National Mall. Despite organizers previously announcing him as a headliner, Day clarified his non-participation in the event.

The Freedom 250 festival is part of a 16-day celebration marking the nation's 250th birthday in Washington. The lineup includes performers such as Martina McBride, Flo Rida, and Vanilla Ice.

cards.headline: Olivia Rodrigo Responds to Criticism Over Recent Fashion Choices
cards.teaser: The singer addressed backlash after internet commenters accused her recent outfits of both infantilizing and sexualizing her.
cards.body:
Olivia Rodrigo weighed in on controversy surrounding her recent clothing. Internet commenters lodged accusations that her recent getups both infantilized and sexualized the singer.

Rodrigo said people should not be responsible for some guy sexualizing them. The star's comments came in response to the dress outrage that emerged online over her fashion choices.

cards.headline: Jimmy Kimmel Calls Adam Carolla His Life Partner at Walk of Fame Ceremony
cards.teaser: The late-night host became emotional while honoring his longtime friend and former colleague at the Hollywood Walk of Fame event.
cards.body:
Jimmy Kimmel became emotional while celebrating Adam Carolla's Hollywood Walk of Fame star on Wednesday. He called Carolla his life partner and made a lighthearted joke about the phrasing, saying "if that sounds gay to you, it was and it is."

Kimmel traced their connection back to 1994, when he was working on the Los Angeles radio show Kevin and Bean alongside Carolla. The two have remained close friends and professional collaborators throughout their careers in entertainment.

hero.headline: U.S. Strikes Iran Military Targets for Second Time This Week
hero.body:
The United States conducted new strikes on military sites in southern Iran on Wednesday, marking the second such attack in three days. According to U.S. officials, the strikes targeted attack drones and a drone ground control station that Iran had launched.

The military operations were described as defensive in nature. Officials stated the attacks focused on four one-way attack drones, hitting military installations in Iran's southern region.

The strikes come while diplomatic negotiations between Washington and Tehran continue, though a cease-fire between the countries remains fragile. The two nations have been engaged in talks aimed at resolving a three-month conflict that has involved multiple regional actors. The latest military operations threaten to complicate these ongoing diplomatic efforts, even as negotiations have stretched over an extended period without producing a final agreement.

Iran's foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, said his government expects to have a draft counterproposal ready within days following nuclear talks with the U.S. this week. During indirect discussions in Geneva with Trump's special envoy Steve Witkoff and son-in-law Jared Kushner, Araghchi stated the sides had reached an understanding on main "guiding principles." He indicated more talks could occur in about a week.

President Trump has signaled he is considering limited military strikes to pressure Iran into making concessions on its nuclear program. He ordered a massive buildup of naval forces in the Middle East, including repositioning aircraft carriers and other warships. Trump gave Iran a deadline of 10 to 15 days to make a deal or face "really bad things."

Araghchi countered that there is no "military solution" to Iran's nuclear program. "That has been tested last year," he said, referring to strikes on Iranian facilities. "They couldn't kill our nuclear programme."

During Geneva discussions, the U.S. did not seek zero uranium enrichment and Iran did not offer to suspend enrichment. Araghchi explained the focus shifted to ensuring Iran's nuclear program remains peaceful. A White House official responded that "the president has been clear that Iran cannot have nuclear weapons or the capacity to build them, and that they cannot enrich uranium."

Oil markets responded to the strikes with price increases, as traders expressed renewed concerns about potential disruptions to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. The waterway is critical for global energy supplies.

The conflict has affected neighboring countries. Kuwait reported being targeted by missiles and drones, though no attribution was provided. Israel has intensified military operations in southern Lebanon during the same period, with Lebanese residents expressing doubt that any U.S.-Iran agreement would bring peace to their country.

cards.headline: Uganda Closes Border With Congo as Ebola Cases Rise
cards.teaser: Uganda shut its border with the Democratic Republic of Congo after Ebola cases were confirmed in the capital Kampala.
cards.body:
Uganda closed its border with the Democratic Republic of Congo amid a worsening Ebola outbreak in the eastern region. Suspected cases in the DRC have exceeded 900, with 119 suspected deaths reported. The World Health Organization has assessed the outbreak as posing a "very high" risk within the country, though it notes the global spread risk remains low.

Uganda has confirmed seven Ebola cases in Kampala, the capital. The country has implemented disease surveillance systems to monitor the situation and prevent further transmission across the border.

cards.headline: Record Spring Heat Wave Breaks Temperature Records Across Europe
cards.teaser: An unusually early heat wave shattered records in multiple European capitals, bringing deaths and prompting emergency responses.
cards.body:
Western Europe is experiencing an exceptionally early heat wave that has shattered spring temperature records across the continent. London has recorded temperatures reaching 95 degrees over consecutive days, triggering government warnings. The extreme conditions have resulted in deaths in several European countries.

Scientists attribute the intense heat to a combination of a heat dome and climate change. The buckled jet stream has created unpredictable and extreme weather patterns that are becoming increasingly frequent. Experts warn that these record-breaking temperatures represent a troubling trend of escalating heat events.

cards.headline: Iran Restores Internet Access After 88-Day Shutdown
cards.teaser: The Iranian government allowed citizens to reconnect with the outside world after nearly three months of censored communications.
cards.body:
Iran ended a near-total internet shutdown that had lasted 88 days, allowing its population to access online services again. The government had blocked television, chat services, and most internet connectivity during the period.

Access remains uneven across the country, with not all Iranians able to connect. Citizens who have regained internet access expressed uncertainty about whether the government would maintain the restored connectivity or impose new restrictions.

cards.headline: Jill Biden Says She Feared Husband Was Having Stroke During 2024 Debate
cards.teaser: The former first lady told CBS News she was frightened by Joe Biden's debate performance against Donald Trump.
cards.body:
Jill Biden told CBS News that she was frightened while watching Joe Biden's performance during his 2024 presidential debate against Donald Trump. The former first lady said she had never seen her husband perform that way before or since.

In the interview set to air on Sunday, Biden expressed concern about what she witnessed, describing her reaction as one of fear during the debate.

cards.headline: Lebanese Expect Prolonged Conflict Despite U.S.-Iran Negotiations
cards.teaser: Residents of Lebanon say diplomatic efforts between Washington and Tehran will not bring peace to their country.
cards.body:
Lebanese citizens expressed skepticism that negotiations between the United States and Iran would end fighting in their country. Clashes between Israel and Hezbollah have intensified in southern Lebanon during the broader regional conflict.

Few in Lebanon believe the diplomatic process will bring peace even if the U.S. and Iran reach an agreement. The fighting in the south has continued despite ongoing talks aimed at ending the wider war.

hero.headline: U.S. strikes Iranian drone site as Trump maintains demands
hero.body:
The United States conducted airstrikes on an Iranian military facility after downing Iranian attack drones, according to U.S. officials. The strikes represent continued military action as President Trump holds firm on what officials describe as maximum demands in negotiations with Tehran.

The timing of the military operations comes as Trump expressed indifference to pressure from some members of his party about conducting strikes before midterm elections. The president has maintained his hardline position on Iran policy despite criticism about potential political consequences.

Trump signaled that he will not lift a naval blockade on Iranian ports until securing a deal addressing Iran's nuclear program. In an interview with Axios, the president said the blockade was more effective than bombing, stating "They are choking like a stuffed pig. And it is going to be worse for them."

This position has had significant economic consequences. Brent crude oil jumped to its highest level in nearly four years, hitting $119.76 a barrel. The price increase reflects market concerns about disruptions to the Strait of Hormuz, a critical shipping channel for global energy supplies. Oil prices rose approximately 7 percent following Trump's comments about extending the blockade.

The blockade's economic impact extends beyond energy markets. The United States has become a net exporter of crude oil for the first time since World War Two, shipping record volumes to international refiners scrambling for supplies. This has led to significant drops in domestic crude oil inventories, according to the Energy Information Administration.

The broader conflict has created economic strain across multiple sectors. Britain's stock market ended at its lowest close since March, with the FTSE 100 dropping 1.16 percent. UK borrowing costs are rising as oil and gas price increases threaten to push up inflation. The yield on two-year UK government bonds hit its highest level since March.

Financial institutions have begun accounting for conflict-related losses. Lloyds Bank took a 151 million pound charge to cover economic damage from the Iran war. Middle East conflicts have also knocked UK exports to the region down by a fifth.

In a contrasting development, pharmaceutical company AstraZeneca announced a surprise 300 million pound investment in the UK. The company said it would unfreeze a paused 200 million pound expansion in Cambridge and invest 100 million pounds into its Macclesfield site. This investment represents a turnaround after the company paused large-scale projects previously.

The decision signals potential recovery in UK life sciences investment. Since a UK-U.S. drug pricing deal reached in December, companies have invested 1.4 billion pounds in UK life sciences. The pharmaceutical industry's trade association described the recent months as "remarkable" for UK life sciences investment.

Talks between Washington and Tehran have continued for three months without breakthrough. Military operations continue alongside diplomatic channels as both sides navigate the conflict.

cards.headline: Former CIA officer arrested with $40 million in gold bars at home
cards.teaser: Federal authorities arrested a former CIA official after discovering approximately 300 gold bars valued at $40 million in his residence.
cards.body:
The FBI arrested David Rush, a former CIA officer, after prosecutors said he stole $40 million worth of gold bars from the agency. Authorities recovered approximately 300 gold bars from his home.

Rush had worked as a government official before his arrest. Federal prosecutors accused him of taking the gold bars from the CIA during his time with the agency. The arrest represents one of the largest alleged thefts of physical assets from a U.S. intelligence organization.

cards.headline: Biden sues Justice Department to block interview recordings
cards.teaser: Former President Joe Biden filed a lawsuit against the Justice Department seeking to prevent the release of audio recordings from interviews.
cards.body:
Biden took legal action to stop the Justice Department from releasing audio files of interviews he gave. The lawsuit represents an unusual step of a former president suing the department he once oversaw.

President Trump criticized Biden over the legal filing, accusing him of trying to hide the interview recordings. The Justice Department has not commented on the substance of the recordings or the timeline for their potential release.

cards.headline: Washington paper mill disaster leaves 11 presumed dead
cards.teaser: A chemical tank rupture at a Longview paper mill may be the deadliest industrial accident in modern Washington state history, according to the governor.
cards.body:
A chemical tank ruptured at a Nippon paper mill in Longview, Washington, resulting in one confirmed death and nine people missing. Nine others sustained injuries in the incident.

The rupture released white liquor, a caustic chemical used in paper production. Washington's governor called the disaster a potential "deadliest industrial tragedy in modern Washington state history."

cards.headline: Google employee charged over $1.2 million in prediction market profits
cards.teaser: The Justice Department charged a Google staffer with using insider information to profit from trades on the prediction market platform Polymarket.
cards.body:
Federal prosecutors charged Google employee Michele Spagnuolo with fraud after he allegedly used insider information to make $1.2 million in profits on Polymarket. According to the unsealed complaint, Spagnuolo had access to Google's confidential data about Search-related trends in 2025, which he used to gain an unfair advantage on the prediction market platform.

This marks the second known federal case involving criminal charges for insider trading on a prediction market site. Polymarket allows users to bet on the outcomes of various future events, from elections to corporate decisions.

hero.headline: Google engineer charged with insider trading after betting $1.2 million on Polymarket
hero.body:
Federal prosecutors in New York charged a longtime Google employee with insider trading after he allegedly used internal company data to place bets worth $1.2 million on the prediction market platform Polymarket.

The engineer worked in information security at Google. Prosecutors allege he accessed confidential information through his position at the company and used that data to inform bets on Polymarket, a platform where users wager on the outcomes of real-world events.

The charges were filed in New York and represent the latest case of authorities targeting alleged misuse of insider information. The case marks an unusual application of insider trading laws to prediction market betting rather than traditional stock trading.

Polymarket operates as a decentralized prediction market where participants bet on outcomes ranging from political elections to economic indicators. The platform has grown in popularity as an alternative way to gauge public sentiment on major events.

Prosecutors did not disclose what specific events the Google employee bet on or what type of internal Google data he allegedly accessed. The charging documents also did not specify the time period during which the alleged trading occurred.

The engineer's employment status at Google following the charges was not made public. Google has not issued a statement about the case or the employee's status with the company.

Insider trading laws traditionally apply to securities markets, where individuals with access to material nonpublic information about publicly traded companies are prohibited from trading on that knowledge. This case extends those principles to prediction markets, where bets function similarly to trades.

The $1.2 million figure represents the total value of bets placed, though it was not clear from available information whether that amount reflected profits, total wagers, or another metric. The specific charges filed against the engineer were not detailed in the available source material.

The case adds to growing regulatory attention on prediction markets and how existing financial laws apply to these newer platforms. Legal experts have debated whether traditional insider trading frameworks adequately cover betting on prediction markets versus conventional securities trading.

cards.headline: Stock markets close at record highs as oil prices fall on Iran war hopes
cards.teaser: The Dow, S&P 500, and Nasdaq all reached record closing levels while oil prices dropped amid expectations for an end to conflict with Iran.
cards.body:
Major US stock indexes reached all-time highs Monday as investors grew optimistic about a potential peace deal between the US and Iran. The Dow Jones Industrial Average, S&P 500, and Nasdaq all posted record closes.

Oil prices tumbled during the session, with Brent crude futures falling 6% to $97.43 a barrel—the lowest level in two weeks—as hopes for an agreement to end the nearly three-month conflict strengthened. Micron Technology extended its gains amid continued momentum in artificial intelligence stocks.

cards.headline: Court orders customs chief to appear over $166 billion in tariff refunds
cards.teaser: A judge demanded the customs chief address compliance issues related to repaying tariffs that were ruled illegal.
cards.body:
A court ordered the head of US Customs to appear at a hearing to address the Trump administration's efforts to refund $166 billion in tariffs that were imposed illegally. The demand for testimony indicated new judicial concern about compliance with refund requirements.

The refunds stem from tariffs that courts determined violated the law. The hearing requirement represented an escalation in judicial oversight of the refund process, with the judge seeking direct answers from the customs chief about the administration's progress in returning the money.

cards.headline: Ferrari faces backlash over first electric car
cards.teaser: The Italian automaker's initial electric vehicle sparked criticism in Italy and beyond, with memes mocking the model and investors selling stock.
cards.body:
Ferrari's unveiling of its first fully electric car, the Luce model, has sparked significant backlash. The new model divided opinion on social media, with memes mocking the vehicle. Analysts questioned its market appeal, and investors responded by selling Ferrari stock.

The negative reaction reflects broader concerns about the brand's shift away from high-performance gasoline engines. A former Ferrari chairman warned about "the destruction of a legend," highlighting worries that electrification could damage Ferrari's iconic status in the automotive world.

cards.headline: FIFA investigated over World Cup ticket prices and sales practices
cards.teaser: New York and New Jersey authorities are examining the soccer association after reports that fans were misled about ticket sales and seating.
cards.body:
The attorneys general of New York and New Jersey have launched a joint investigation into FIFA's ticketing practices for the 2026 World Cup. The probe focuses on matches scheduled for MetLife Stadium in East Rutherford, New Jersey, and was announced by New York's Letitia James and New Jersey's Jennifer Davenport.

Fans have reported being misled about seat locations, and authorities are examining whether FIFA's public messaging contributed to inflated ticket prices. The investigation involves a subpoena seeking information about FIFA's ticketing practices and how the organization marketed and sold World Cup tickets to buyers.

hero.headline: Australia sues 3M for $2 billion over contaminated firefighting foam
hero.body:
The Australian government filed a lawsuit against US manufacturing giant 3M seeking $2 billion in damages over contamination caused by PFAS chemicals in firefighting foam used at dozens of defense sites across the country.

The case centers on per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances, commonly known as PFAS or "forever chemicals," which were present in foam products supplied by 3M. These chemicals earned their nickname because they do not break down naturally in the environment and can persist for decades.

The contamination affected multiple Australian defense facilities where the foam had been deployed. PFAS chemicals have raised health and environmental concerns globally due to their resistance to degradation and their accumulation in soil, water, and living organisms.

The $2 billion lawsuit represents one of the largest legal actions taken by a national government against 3M over PFAS contamination. The company has faced similar litigation in multiple countries as awareness of the chemicals' environmental persistence has grown.

3M, headquartered in Minnesota, manufactures a wide range of industrial and consumer products. The company previously produced firefighting foams containing PFAS for use by military installations, airports, and fire departments around the world.

Australian defense sites used these foam products for firefighting and training exercises over many years. The legal action alleges that this use resulted in widespread contamination of soil and groundwater at the affected locations.

The lawsuit comes as governments worldwide have increased scrutiny of PFAS chemicals and their manufacturers. Several countries have moved to phase out or restrict the use of these substances in firefighting foam and other products.

3M announced in recent years that it would discontinue manufacturing PFAS-based products, though the timeline for complete phase-out varies by product line and region. The company has also faced cleanup costs and legal settlements related to PFAS contamination at sites in the United States and other countries.

The Australian government's legal action seeks to recover costs associated with investigating and remediating the contamination at defense facilities. The case will proceed through Australian courts, though no trial date has been announced.

cards.headline: Rivian sets June 9 delivery date for first R2 electric SUVs
cards.teaser: The electric vehicle maker will begin customer deliveries of its new R2 SUV on June 9.
cards.body:
Rivian has set June 9 as the delivery date for the first R2 electric SUVs to customers. The company has been working toward this milestone for its newest model.

CEO RJ Scaringe has called the R2 "maybe the most important thing we've launched to date," underscoring its significance to the company's expansion plans.

cards.headline: California court rejects Tesla bid to dismiss racial discrimination lawsuit
cards.teaser: A California court denied Tesla's attempt to throw out a racial discrimination lawsuit brought by state civil rights officials.
cards.body:
A California court denied Tesla's motion to dismiss a racial discrimination lawsuit brought by the state's civil rights agency. The ruling clears the path for the case to advance to trial, with proceedings expected to begin in July.

The civil rights agency views the court's decision as a significant victory in its legal challenge against the electric vehicle manufacturer over allegations of racial discrimination at Tesla facilities.

cards.headline: NASA spacecraft captures detailed Mars images during flyby
cards.teaser: A NASA probe photographed Mars in high resolution while passing the planet on its journey to study a distant asteroid.
cards.body:
NASA's Psyche spacecraft captured detailed images of Mars during a flyby on its way to explore a metal-rich asteroid in the outer solar system. The photographs showcase the Martian south pole and other surface features from a unique vantage point.

The high-resolution images provide scientists with valuable data to study as Psyche continues its multi-year journey toward its primary mission target, the asteroid it was designed to investigate.

cards.headline: Nintendo adds Donkey Kong 64 to Switch Online next week
cards.teaser: The classic Nintendo 64 game Donkey Kong 64 will join the Switch Online library next week.
cards.body:
Nintendo announced it will add Donkey Kong 64 to its Nintendo Switch Online service next week, expanding the platform's collection of classic Nintendo 64 titles. The 1999 adventure game will become available to subscribers who pay for the service tier that includes retro games.

Donkey Kong 64 originally released for the Nintendo 64 console and featured the barrel-throwing ape in a three-dimensional platforming adventure. The addition continues Nintendo's gradual expansion of vintage games available through its online subscription service.

hero.headline: Georgia coach suggests SEC could leave NCAA over playoff dispute
hero.body:
Georgia head coach Kirby Smart indicated the Southeastern Conference could separate from the NCAA if the league cannot reach an agreement on College Football Playoff terms. Smart made the comments during SEC spring meetings, where conference expansion has dominated discussions.

The possibility of SEC secession emerged as the league debates its future in college athletics governance. The conference has faced challenges in recent playoff negotiations, including a 4-0 record against them by Big Ten teams in head-to-head College Football Playoff matchups over the past three seasons.

SEC Commissioner Greg Sankey has maintained the conference still stands alone despite the Big Ten winning the past three national titles. The competitive landscape has shifted as conference realignment reshapes college football.

Smart's suggestion that the SEC could operate under its own rules reflects broader tensions in college athletics. The spring meetings have turned into what observers describe as a reality check for the current structure of college sports governance.

The comments come as multiple reports indicate the SEC is evaluating its options for future governance structures. The conference would seek to establish its own competitive framework if it cannot secure favorable terms in playoff negotiations.

College Football Playoff expansion remains a central issue in these discussions. Oklahoma athletic director Roger Denny separately noted that playoff expansion could enable scheduling tougher nonconference games and potentially revive rivalry series like the Sooners' matchup against Oklahoma State.

The potential departure would represent a fundamental restructuring of college athletics. The SEC has not provided a timeline for any decision, but Smart's public statements signal the league is prepared to consider alternatives to NCAA membership if necessary.

cards.headline: Hurricanes take 3-1 series lead with shutout win over Canadiens
cards.teaser: Frederik Andersen made 18 saves as Carolina moved within one win of the Stanley Cup Final.
cards.body:
Goaltender Frederik Andersen delivered a dominant performance, making 18 saves to shut out the Canadiens and push the Hurricanes within one win of the Stanley Cup Final. The victory gave Carolina a 3-1 series lead in the Eastern Conference Final.

Andersen's shutout marked his third of the postseason. The Hurricanes can clinch their trip to the Finals with a win in Game 5.

cards.headline: Phillies pitcher sets franchise record with 44 consecutive scoreless innings
cards.teaser: Cristopher Sanchez broke a record held by Hall of Famer Grover Cleveland Alexander since 1911.
cards.body:
Cristopher Sánchez set a new Phillies franchise record on Wednesday, extending his scoreless innings streak to 44⅔ innings. He surpassed the previous mark held by Hall of Famer Grover Cleveland Alexander, who set the original record in 1911.

Sánchez's achievement represents the longest scoreless streak in Phillies history across the franchise's 115-year existence.

cards.headline: Projected first-round pick Koa Peat stays in NBA draft
cards.teaser: The Arizona forward will forgo his remaining college eligibility.
cards.body:
Arizona forward Koa Peat has declared for the NBA draft, according to ESPN sources. The decision on Wednesday means he is forgoing his remaining college eligibility to pursue a professional basketball career.

Peat is expected to be selected in the first round of the upcoming draft.

cards.headline: Former Super Bowl MVP Von Miller seeks return to Broncos
cards.teaser: The linebacker said he has lobbied Denver coach Sean Payton about rejoining his former team.
cards.body:
Von Miller declared Wednesday that he will definitely play in the 2026 season and has already reached out to Denver Broncos coach Sean Payton about a potential reunion. The Super Bowl MVP is actively pursuing a return to his former team.

Miller's direct approach to the Broncos coaching staff shows his clear interest in rejoining the franchise where he previously won his championship.

cards.headline: Top transfer portal player Milan Momcilovic withdraws from NBA draft
cards.teaser: The former Iowa State forward will return to college basketball next season.
cards.body:
Milan Momcilovic is withdrawing from the NBA draft to continue his college basketball career. The forward, who previously played for Iowa State, was ranked as the top player available in the transfer portal.

After declaring for the NBA draft, Momcilovic decided to return to college rather than pursue a professional career. His agents confirmed the decision to ESPN.

hero.headline: Spielberg Says Hollywood Should Never Use AI as Final Word on Creative Decisions
hero.body:
Steven Spielberg spoke out against artificial intelligence in filmmaking during an appearance on Michelle Obama and Craig Robinson's IMO podcast. The director said he opposes AI taking over the creative process in Hollywood.

Spielberg drew a clear line on where he finds AI acceptable. He said the technology can be useful for finding solutions to medical issues. However, he does not want it controlling creative decisions in film production.

The director stated that AI should never serve as the final word on anything creative. He identified this boundary as his primary concern with the technology's role in entertainment.

Spielberg's comments add his voice to ongoing debates in Hollywood about AI's expanding role in the industry. His position reflects concern among filmmakers about preserving human creativity and decision-making in the production process.

The legendary director's remarks come as AI tools become increasingly sophisticated and more widely available to studios and production companies. Various forms of AI are already being used in script analysis, visual effects, and other aspects of filmmaking.

Spielberg has directed numerous acclaimed films over a career spanning more than five decades. His stance carries significant weight in industry discussions about the future of filmmaking technology and creative control.

cards.headline: ABC News and National Geographic Lead News Emmy Awards
cards.teaser: ABC World News Tonight won outstanding live news program for the second consecutive year at the 47th annual News Emmys.
cards.body:
ABC News dominated the 47th annual News Emmy Awards with eight wins, capturing the top prize for outstanding live news program. ABC World News Tonight with David Muir secured the award for the second consecutive year.

National Geographic achieved strong recognition at the ceremony with seven News Emmy Awards. The outlet's wins were highlighted by honors for Trafficked with Mariana van Zeller, underscoring the Disney-owned network's competitive performance in television news.

cards.headline: Student Journalist Criticizes CBS News While Accepting Mike Wallace Scholarship
cards.teaser: Santiago Campos called out CBS News during his acceptance speech at the News Emmys, saying the outlet's recent direction damages Mike Wallace's legacy.
cards.body:
Santiago Campos, a senior at District of Columbia International School in Washington, addressed CBS News critically while accepting the Mike Wallace Memorial Scholarship at the News Emmy Awards. The scholarship is named after the veteran CBS journalist.

Former CBS Evening News anchor Scott Pelley presented the award. Campos told the crowd that the recent direction of CBS News stains the legacy of Mike Wallace. The student's remarks drew attention from the News Emmy audience.

cards.headline: Morris Day Denies Planned Appearance at National Mall Freedom 250 Concert
cards.teaser: The singer said he will not perform at a patriotic festival in Washington despite being listed as a headliner by event organizers.
cards.body:
Morris Day has denied rumors that he and the Time will perform at the Freedom 250 concert scheduled for June 27 on the National Mall. Despite organizers previously announcing him as a headliner, Day clarified his non-participation in the event.

The Freedom 250 festival is part of a 16-day celebration marking the nation's 250th birthday in Washington. The lineup includes performers such as Martina McBride, Flo Rida, and Vanilla Ice.

cards.headline: Olivia Rodrigo Responds to Criticism Over Recent Fashion Choices
cards.teaser: The singer addressed backlash after internet commenters accused her recent outfits of both infantilizing and sexualizing her.
cards.body:
Olivia Rodrigo weighed in on controversy surrounding her recent clothing. Internet commenters lodged accusations that her recent getups both infantilized and sexualized the singer.

Rodrigo said people should not be responsible for some guy sexualizing them. The star's comments came in response to the dress outrage that emerged online over her fashion choices.

cards.headline: Jimmy Kimmel Calls Adam Carolla His Life Partner at Walk of Fame Ceremony
cards.teaser: The late-night host became emotional while honoring his longtime friend and former colleague at the Hollywood Walk of Fame event.
cards.body:
Jimmy Kimmel became emotional while celebrating Adam Carolla's Hollywood Walk of Fame star on Wednesday. He called Carolla his life partner and made a lighthearted joke about the phrasing, saying "if that sounds gay to you, it was and it is."

Kimmel traced their connection back to 1994, when he was working on the Los Angeles radio show Kevin and Bean alongside Carolla. The two have remained close friends and professional collaborators throughout their careers in entertainment.

hero.headline: Justice Department opens criminal investigation into Trump accuser E. Jean Carroll
hero.body:
The Department of Justice has launched a criminal investigation into E. Jean Carroll, who accused President Trump of sexual assault, according to multiple reports.

CNN first reported Wednesday night that the investigation focuses on whether Carroll committed perjury while speaking at a deposition during her two civil lawsuits against Trump. The probe represents a significant escalation in the legal battle between Carroll and the president.

Carroll won two civil cases against Trump. In the first case, a jury found Trump liable for sexual abuse and defamation. In the second case, a jury awarded Carroll additional damages for defamation after Trump continued to deny her allegations.

The criminal investigation comes as Trump has repeatedly denied Carroll's accusations and criticized the civil verdicts against him. The Justice Department has not publicly commented on the scope or timeline of the investigation.

Perjury charges require prosecutors to prove that a witness knowingly made false statements under oath during official proceedings. The penalty for perjury in federal court can include fines and imprisonment.

Carroll originally came forward in 2019 with allegations that Trump sexually assaulted her in a department store dressing room in the mid-1990s. Trump denied the allegations and said he had never met Carroll, despite a photograph showing them together.

The civil trials included testimony from both Carroll and Trump, as well as other witnesses. Carroll testified under oath during depositions and at trial about her allegations and the impact of Trump's public denials.

The investigation adds another layer to the ongoing legal confrontations between Trump and his accusers. It also raises questions about the Justice Department's independence, as the agency now investigates someone who successfully sued the current president in civil court.

Neither the Justice Department nor Carroll's legal team has made public statements about the investigation. The timing and potential outcomes of the probe remain uncertain.

cards.headline: Former judges ask court to review Trump IRS settlement creating $1.776 billion fund
cards.teaser: A bipartisan group of former federal judges asked a court to reopen a case involving President Trump's lawsuit against the IRS.
cards.body:
A bipartisan group of former federal judges asked a federal court Wednesday to investigate President Trump's settlement with the Internal Revenue Service. The judges argue that the administration bypassed proper judicial oversight by negotiating the deal outside of court proceedings.

The settlement established a $1.776 billion fund intended to compensate alleged victims of what the administration calls "lawfare and weaponization." California Governor Gavin Newsom announced plans to impose a 100% tax on any payments received by state residents from the fund, seeking to prevent the money from reaching Trump allies and others he views as undeserving recipients.

cards.headline: US military shoots down four Iranian drones, strikes ground station
cards.teaser: American forces intercepted Iranian attack drones targeting a commercial ship and destroyed a drone launch facility.
cards.body:
The U.S. military intercepted four Iranian attack drones and destroyed a ground control station in Bandar Abbas that was preparing to launch a fifth drone. The drones threatened a commercial vessel in the Strait of Hormuz.

This represents the second military engagement between U.S. and Iranian forces within 48 hours, occurring amid ongoing negotiations between the two countries during a fragile ceasefire in the three-month conflict.

cards.headline: Appeals court allows pro-Palestinian activist to remain free pending Supreme Court appeal
cards.teaser: A federal appeals panel ruled that Mahmoud Khalil can stay out of custody while challenging his case.
cards.body:
A three-judge panel of the 3rd Circuit Court of Appeals ruled Tuesday that pro-Palestinian activist Mahmoud Khalil can remain free as he takes his case against the Trump administration to the Supreme Court. The panel includes appointees from three different administrations.

Judges Stephanos Bibas, Arianna Freeman and Thomas Hardiman issued the order. Bibas was appointed by President Trump, Freeman by former President George W. Bush, and Hardiman by former President Joe Biden.

cards.headline: Senator Andy Kim responds to Homeland Security secretary over detention facility protest
cards.teaser: The New Jersey senator pushed back after being criticized for attending a demonstration outside a migrant facility.
cards.body:
Democratic Sen. Andy Kim of New Jersey responded Wednesday to criticism from Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, who slammed the senator for attending a protest outside a migrant detention facility in New Jersey. During a cabinet meeting at the White House, Mullin said Kim complained about being hit by pepper ball spray at the protest.

Kim fired back at the secretary's comments, stating that the incident was not about him personally. The exchange highlighted tensions between Democratic lawmakers and the Trump administration over immigration enforcement policies.

cards.headline: Senate Republicans move to support Paxton after divisive Texas primary
cards.teaser: Republican leadership is working to unite the party behind Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton following his primary victory.
cards.body:
Senate Republican leaders are working to rebuild their relationship with Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton following a contentious primary battle. Senate Majority Leader John Thune of South Dakota spoke with Paxton by phone and subsequently endorsed him on a radio show, while also criticizing the Democratic nominee for state attorney general.

The primary contest between Paxton and Sen. John Cornyn was expensive and divisive, costing $130 million. Party leadership now considers Texas essential to their efforts to maintain control of the Senate, prompting senior Republicans to signal their support to major donors.
